introduction:
Antimicrobial Peptides (AMPs) are a class of biologically active peptides with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, playing a key role in the immune defense of organisms [1, 2]. In the face of the escalating problem of antibiotic resistance, AMPs have become a major research focus thanks to their unique antimicrobial mechanisms, lower risk of inducing drug resistance, and broad specificity [3, 4]. However, traditional discovery methods are complex, costly, and inefficient, failing to meet the urgent demand for novel AMPs [5]. Consequently, researchers have increasingly turned to computational methods [6], with machine learning approaches achieving significant milestones [7]. Early methods often relied on conventional algorithms such as Random Forest (RF) [8–11], Support Vector Machines (SVM) [12–15], and ensemble learning methods [16, 17]. A common limitation of these methods is their reliance on handcrafted features, which requires domain expertise and restricts their universality and scalability.
Deep learning overcomes these limitations by leveraging multi-layer neural network architectures to automatically learn and extract high-level, abstract features from raw sequence data [18–22], significantly advancing the computational prediction of AMPs. This paradigm encompasses various architectures. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) [23, 24] excel at capturing local motifs, while Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) [25, 26] and their variants like LSTM [27, 28] are used to model sequential context and long-range dependencies. More recently, the Transformer architecture [29], with its self-attention mechanism, and its derivative large language models (such as BERT [30] and ESM [31]) have become the dominant paradigm, establishing a new standard for protein and peptide representation learning and function prediction due to their outstanding sequence modeling capabilities.
Concurrently, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for modeling complex relationships between entities [32]. For instance, LABAMP [33] constructs a graph containing sequence nodes and k-mer nodes (e.g., tripeptides). The framework then leverages a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) to learn node representations for identifying bacteriocins. A different and prominent line of work focuses on the internal structure of individual peptides. The sAMPpred-GAT [34] model begins by predicting the contact map of each peptide using trRosetta. It then constructs an individual intra-molecular graph where nodes are amino acids and edges represent their spatial proximity based on the predicted residue distances. A Graph Attention Network (GAT) is then used to learn discriminative features from these structural graphs. Building on this structure-based approach, TP-LMMSG [35] innovates on the node feature representation by employing pre-trained language models. In a separate work, Cordoves-Delgado et al. [36] construct graphs from ESMFold-predicted 3D structures, while leveraging ESM-2 embeddings for amino acid-level features. Similarly, PepTriX [37] employs ESMFold-predicted structures with a GAT enhanced by contrastive training and cross-modal co-attention. However, these structure-based approaches share a common limitation: they require computationally expensive 3D structure prediction as a prerequisite step, and their graph construction is confined to individual peptides without capturing inter-sequence relationships.
In this work, we propose a novel framework PepGraphormer that combines the powers of transformer-based LLMs and GNNs for antimicrobial peptide prediction. Unlike previous GNN-based methods, PepGraphormer bypasses 3D structure prediction entirely, eliminating the substantial computational burden associated with auxiliary folding algorithms and avoiding the inherent noise and bias introduced by the potentially low-confidence structural predictions of short, flexible peptides.. PepGraphormer constructs a single, inter-molecular, heterogeneous graph that covers the entire dataset. In this graph, edges are defined not by physical distance but by statistical relationships: Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) [38] for sequence-to-amino-acid edges, and Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) [39] for amino-acid-to-amino-acid edges. PepGraphormer is designed to synergistically leverage the powerful feature extraction capabilities from ESM2 and the relational dependencies learned by a GAT from the graph, aiming to enhance the accuracy and robustness of peptide function prediction. Experimental results show that PepGraphormer outperforms or performs comparably to current SOTA methods on seven benchmark datasets and demonstrates strong generalization to other therapeutic peptide prediction tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lincubator/PepGraphormer.

PepGraphormer integrates a protein language model with a GAT to improve AMP prediction performance. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the process begins with an input peptide sequence, which is encoded by the ESM2 model. The resulting sequence-level feature vector serves a dual purpose: it acts as the initial representation for the corresponding sequence node in the GAT network, and provides a partial prediction based on the sequence information. The GAT operates on a heterogeneous graph composed of sequence nodes and amino acid nodes. It employs a multi-head attention mechanism to learn the importance of neighboring nodes, aggregating feature information from multi-hop neighborhoods to integrate both local context and global structural dependencies. Finally, the model's prediction results from the fusion of ESM2's deep semantic understanding and the GAT's learned relational features. PepGraphormer constructs a heterogeneous graph comprising sequence nodes (representing peptides) and amino acid nodes (representing single residues). The graph's edges are strategically weighted by two principles to capture both local and global information. First, sequence-to-amino-acid edges are weighted using TF-IDF [38] to define the distinctive amino acid composition of each local peptide. Second, amino-acid-to-amino-acid edges are weighted based on PMI [39] to model the global statistical co-occurrence between residue pairs across the entire dataset. This dual-edge strategy is designed to reveal key amino acid motifs and underlying functional associations, providing a rich semantic foundation for pattern propagation from labeled to unlabeled sequences. To ensure an objective evaluation of the model's predictive performance, we not only adopted the datasets previously used by Xu et al. [42], sAMPpred-GAT [34], and TP-LMMSG [35], but also strictly adhered to the data processing protocols established in these benchmark studies to eliminate potential bias.. For these datasets, the positive samples were comprehensively curated from typical AMP databases, including SATPdb [43], ADAM [44], AMPfun [10], APD3 [45], CAMP [46, 47], LAMP [48, 49], DRAMP [50], and dbAMP [51]. The curation process involved removing sequences with non-standard residues and retaining only those with lengths between 11 and 100 amino acids. Furthermore, to mitigate biases from sequence homology and redundancy, CD-HIT [52] was employed to reduce the sequence identity to a 90% threshold [28] both within each dataset and against any positive samples in the independent test sets.
For the negative samples, non-antimicrobial peptide sequences were selected from the UniProt [53] by excluding entries containing keywords such as “antimicrobial” or “antibacterial”. These sequences underwent the same cleaning and length-filtering process. CD-HIT was similarly used to reduce sequence identity to a 40% threshold [28] among the negative samples within each dataset and against the independent test sets. The XUAMP dataset was compiled from the other six datasets. Additionally, to validate the model's ability to generalize to other therapeutic peptides, the imbalanced Antiviral Peptide (AVP) and Anticancer Peptide (ACP) datasets, as compiled in TP-LMMSG [35], were also included in our experiments. For data partitioning, we adopted the same training and independent test set splits as established in prior benchmark studies [34, 35, 42]. To ensure an objective evaluation of the model's predictive performance, we not only adopted the datasets previously used by Xu et al. [42], sAMPpred-GAT [34], and TP-LMMSG [35], but also strictly adhered to the data processing protocols established in these benchmark studies to eliminate potential bias.. For these datasets, the positive samples were comprehensively curated from typical AMP databases, including SATPdb [43], ADAM [44], AMPfun [10], APD3 [45], CAMP [46, 47], LAMP [48, 49], DRAMP [50], and dbAMP [51]. The curation process involved removing sequences with non-standard residues and retaining only those with lengths between 11 and 100 amino acids. Furthermore, to mitigate biases from sequence homology and redundancy, CD-HIT [52] was employed to reduce the sequence identity to a 90% threshold [28] both within each dataset and against any positive samples in the independent test sets.
For the negative samples, non-antimicrobial peptide sequences were selected from the UniProt [53] by excluding entries containing keywords such as “antimicrobial” or “antibacterial”. These sequences underwent the same cleaning and length-filtering process. CD-HIT was similarly used to reduce sequence identity to a 40% threshold [28] among the negative samples within each dataset and against the independent test sets. The XUAMP dataset was compiled from the other six datasets. Additionally, to validate the model's ability to generalize to other therapeutic peptides, the imbalanced Antiviral Peptide (AVP) and Anticancer Peptide (ACP) datasets, as compiled in TP-LMMSG [35], were also included in our experiments. To validate the independent contributions of each module and to determine the optimal fusion strategy for the two key components—the ESM2-based prediction and the GAT-based prediction—we designed a series of experiments. In these experiments, we systematically evaluated the model's performance across various metrics while adjusting the fusion factor, m, from 0 to 1 in increments of 0.1. The heatmap in Fig. 4 shows that the model's performance does not increase linearly with m. Instead, it exhibits a fluctuating trend, indicating a search for an optimal balance. The columns corresponding to m = 0.8 and m = 0.9 display the highest overall color intensity, forming a “performance hotspot.” For ACC and MCC—often considered the most important and comprehensive metrics for evaluating a classification model—the values at m = 0.8 (0.7559 and 0.5326, respectively) are the highest across all values of m. The experimental results clearly show that replacing any of PepGraphormer's core components leads to a significant decline in the model's overall performance, validating our choice of ESM2 and GAT. When we replaced ESM2 with Bert (BertGAT), the model's ACC dropped substantially from 0.7552 to 0.7010, while the MCC decreased significantly from 0.5326 to 0.4040. This indicates that ESM2 is more effective than Bert in capturing sequence-level semantic information and is a critical component of the model's high performance. Similarly, when GAT was replaced with GCN (ESMGCN), all key metrics showed a comprehensive decline, with AUC dropping from 0.8149 to 0.7765. This suggests that GAT's attention mechanism more effectively aggregates neighborhood information from the graph structure, contributing more to the model's performance than a standard GCN. When both core modules were replaced simultaneously (BERTGCN), its performance was the lowest among all variants. This result serves as further evidence for the “1 + 1 > 2” synergistic effect between the ESM2 and GAT modules in our architecture. In conclusion, this series of ablation studies demonstrates the rationality and effectiveness of the PepGraphormer architecture.

As illustrated in Fig. 6a, ESM2, by virtue of its powerful pre-training, can already achieve a certain degree of separation between positive samples (AMPs, blue dots) and negative samples (red dots). This indicates that the initial ESM2 embeddings inherently contain semantic information relevant to AMP function. However, a significant overlap region exists between the two classes, resulting in a fuzzy decision boundary. This suggests that relying solely on ESM2's global semantic features for classification has its limitations. In the initial stage of training (Fig. 6b), the GAT module has just begun to learn. At this point, the feature space distribution of the GAT output shows no clear trend of change compared to the initial ESM2 embedding distribution. This is because the GAT's parameters are not yet sufficiently optimized, and the modifying effect of the graph structural information on the original ESM2 features is still negligible. As training progresses (Figs. 6c–e), a significant improvement in the separability of positive and negative sample points is observed in the t-SNE space. The clusters of antimicrobial and non-antimicrobial peptides begin to form more distinct boundaries, and the overlapping region gradually diminishes. This indicates that the GAT is effectively supplementing and refining the original ESM2 embeddings by aggregating neighborhood information, making the sequence representations more discriminative. In the later stages of training (Fig. 6f), the class separability in the feature space reaches a relatively stable and high level. The positive and negative samples have formed two distinct, concentrated clusters with a clear boundary. This visually demonstrates that the GAT module, by propagating and aggregating information on the heterogeneous graph, has successfully learned feature representations that can better distinguish between the different functional peptide sequences.
This series of t-SNE visualizations provides compelling evidence for the effectiveness of PepGraphormer's hybrid architecture. The evolutionary process of the feature space—from an initial mixed state to a final, clearly separated one—visually demonstrates the critical role that the GAT plays in supplementing ESM2's global features and ultimately enhancing the model's predictive performance.
conclusion: This paper introduced PepGraphormer, a deep learning framework that integrates the pre-trained protein language model ESM2 with a Graph Attention Network to predict antimicrobial peptides. Evaluations on public datasets show that PepGraphormer holds a significant advantage over other state-of-the-art models. The effectiveness of its dual-modal fusion architecture was validated through comprehensive ablation studies and generalization experiments. By bypassing 3D structure prediction, PepGraphormer offers an efficient framework for peptide function prediction, potentially accelerating the discovery pipeline for new therapeutic peptides. Future work will focus on optimizing the graph construction strategy and exploring more effective data augmentation techniques. We also plan to extend the framework to multi-label classification for predicting specific antimicrobial activities (e.g., antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral), and investigate transfer learning methods tailored for small-sample scenarios to further enhance performance on small-scale or imbalanced datasets.
